---
title: "Learning curves are not that steep"
format:

    embed-resources: true
execute:
  echo: false

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Fetches the OWID data, fits the lines and builds the plots, leaving them in
# `fits`. It also writes the PNGs and the parameter table, which are ignored.
source("solar-battery-even-axes.R")

# The fit the article shows and quotes
article_method <- "robust"

fitted_plot <- function(series) {
    fits$plot[[which(fits$series == series & fits$method == article_method)]]
}

fit_parameters <- read_csv("line_fit_parameters.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

fitted_slope <- function(series) {
    fit_parameters |>
        filter(
            .data$series == .env$series,
            method == article_method,
            term != "(Intercept)"
        ) |>
        pull(estimate)
}

solar_slope <- fitted_slope("solar")

# One decimal place: the two fitting methods disagree in the second
slope_text <- function(slope) format(round(slope, 1), nsmall = 1)

# How much cumulative production has to grow for the price to fall 10x, to one
# significant figure, which is all the uncertainty in the slope supports
scale_up_text <- function(slope) {
    format(signif(10^(-1 / slope), 1), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)
}
```

In 2024 I was posting about the astonishing progress in solar power.
It was [the year of the big battery](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/mnaEgW9JgiochnES2/2024-was-the-year-of-the-big-battery-and-what-that-means-for).
People were telling me, first of all, that fossil fuels were obsolete for electricity generation.
And second, that for carbon-free electricity generation, nuclear was no longer worthwhile.

I had been converted to a solar believer by the progress in batteries, but I was skeptical of the visions of Solartopia, where we run on solar all day and batteries all night.
I think my skepticism has aged well, as data centers install natural gas turbines and hyperscalers work to restart nuclear plants.
But the basis of my skepticism then was that [batteries were being used for a specific niche use, and that their price would have to drop substantially to escape that niche](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/mnaEgW9JgiochnES2/2024-was-the-year-of-the-big-battery-and-what-that-means-for).

Of course, the astonishing price drops in both solar and batteries are what made us all into solar believers.
The graph of the moment was a "learning curve", showing how price decreases as a function of cumulative production: how many watts of solar cells have ever been produced, or kWh of lithium-ion batteries).
[When such a "curve" is a straight line on a log-log plot, that's an instance of Wright's law](https://ourworldindata.org/learning-curve).
[I have heard it said that Wright's law-based extrapolations are more reliable than extrapolations of Moore's law type](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0052669).

What irritated me about the discourse, though, was the prevalent idea that if you believed in extrapolating these lines, then you believed Solartopia was nigh: we would soon be running on solar all day and batteries all night, and all other energy technologies were dead ends.
For some record that this idea was in the air, see Scott Alexander's [Notes from a Progress Studies Conference](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/notes-from-the-progress-studies-conference).

The problem with this is that the learning curves are not actually that steep.
Even taking for granted that we can extrapolate the learning curve with a Wright's Law-style fit, what these graphs really show is the massive scale of the effort required for each price decrease.

## Solar learning curve

Let's take another look at the Wright's Law learning curve for solar.
Using [OWID data](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/solar-pv-prices-vs-cumulative-capacity), plotting the price of solar power as a function of cumulative capacity:

```{r}
#| label: solar-wrights-law
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Log-log plot of solar module cost against cumulative capacity, with a fitted straight line sloping downwards. Orders of magnitude are the same size on both axes."
fitted_plot("solar")
```

Of course the most impressive thing about this plot is the massive reduction in price, across multiple orders of magnitude.
But notice there are more orders of magnitude on the x-axis than on the y-axis.
I've made sure that orders of magnitude are the same size on both axes, so we can get a visual sense of the relationship.

The slope of the line fit is about `r slope_text(solar_slope)`.
This means a 10x reduction in price requires a scale-up of about `r scale_up_text(solar_slope)`x in cumulative capacity.
That's how hard people fought for every order of magnitude in price reduction.

## Reconsidering solar vs nuclear

Solar is already so cheap that we would be using it for everything if we could easily store and transmit it.
What was new in 2024 was the boom in battery storage, driven by [a similar trend for batteries](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/battery-price-vs-cumulative-production).
Batteries will be much cheaper too, once more factories are built, and have produced many times more battery capacity than has ever existed.
Eventually they will be cheap enough that it's economical to discharge batteries all night at current electricity prices.

But let's reconsider the comparison to nuclear, keeping in mind the massive investment and engineering effort that such a battery scale-up involves.
It's not easy to build a nuclear plant.
Europe's newest nuclear plant, the Flamanville reactor, was a particular embarassment to nuclear, getting far behind schedule and over budget.
But in Europe they can't seem to build battery factories either, as we can see with [Northvolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northvolt).
In China, where they can build solar and battery factories, they can also build nuclear plants, [adding nuclear generation every year, though solar is growing far faster](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/electricity-production-by-source?country=~CHN).
[China also has a small nuclear reactor](https://www.nucnet.org/news/hot-testing-begins-at-china-s-linglong-1-small-modular-reactor-10-3-2026), and if they begin factory production of SMRs, we could see price learning curves for nuclear too.
The effort of starting the SMR industry from nothing seems massive, but producing many times more battery cells than have ever been produced is also a massive effort.
Compare one massive effort to another, and imagine both happening in China, and I think it is not so clear which will be the better option for zero-carbon all-night power.

I think this is what extrapolating the line should look like.
The line tells you what it takes to achieve each price reduction.
Look at the slope, and compare like to like in terms of investment and engineering effort.
